elements: near-end parabolic cross section (deep, narrow U-shaped curve) at the left, open at top, narrowing to a rounded point at the bottom
far-end parabolic cross section at the right, offset along the receding diagonal
straight edges joining the top rims of both ends and the bottom tangent lines, forming the long open channel body
flat water-surface rectangle spanning the opening between the two ends, its width set by the parabola at the current fill depth
horizontal water fill line inside the near-end cross section with translucent blue water below it
double-headed vertical arrow inside the near end from rim to lowest point labeled '18 in'
label '3 ft' along the upper front length edge
label '12 in' across the top width of the far end
cross-section graph view: 2D axes (width x in inches horizontal, depth y vertical) with the fitted parabola y = x^2/2 through points (-6,18) and (6,18), vertex at origin

interactions.label: Water depth h (in)
interactions.teaches: The width of the water surface is a function of depth: as the fill line rises along the parabola y = x^2/2, the surface widens as 2*sqrt(2h), so surface area is not constant with depth

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Switching to the cross-section graph shows how the physical dimensions (18 in deep, 12 in across the top) fit the parabola y = x^2/2 through (-6,18) and (6,18), connecting the physical trough to its equation

interactions.label: Trough length L (ft)
interactions.teaches: Stretching the length extends the water-surface rectangle while the cross-section stays fixed, showing that surface area = width(h) x L multiplies a depth-dependent width by an independent length

interactions.label: Cross-section profile
interactions.teaches: Editing the parabolic profile reshapes both the cross-section graph and the 3D trough fill, so the learner sees that the water width at any depth is derived from the entered curve, not assumed

demo_steps.title: The trough at half depth
demo_steps.narration: The 3 ft trough is filled to h = 9 in. The blue water surface is noticeably narrower than the 12 in top rim — the width of the surface depends on the depth.

demo_steps.title: Fill to the top
demo_steps.narration: Raise the depth to 18 in. The water surface now spans the full 12 in top width, matching the labeled dimension on the far end.

demo_steps.title: Fit the cross-section
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the cross-section graph: with the vertex at the origin, the parabola y = ax^2 passes through (6, 18), so 18 = a·36 gives a = 1/2 and the profile is y = x^2/2. The fill line at depth h shows width 2*sqrt(2h).

demo_steps.title: Change the length
demo_steps.narration: Back in 3D, extend the trough to 6 ft. The cross-section and water width are unchanged; only the surface rectangle lengthens, doubling the water's surface area.

plan.geometry_notes: Work in inches for the cross section, feet for length (1 ft = 12 in). Cross section: parabola y = x^2/2 with vertex (0,0), depth 18, top half-width 6 (top width 12) — verify: y(6) = 36/2 = 18, exactly the labeled depth, and the rim width at y=18 is 2*6 = 12, exactly the labeled top width. Draw the cross section DEEP AND NARROW like the source: world scale 1 in = 0.1 units, so the near-end U-curve is about 1.2 world units wide (12 in) and 1.8 units tall (18 in) — taller than it is wide; do not stretch it horizontally. Near end at the left, drawn true; far end offset up-and-to-the-right along the oblique diagonal at roughly 30 degrees, offset length proportional to L (3 ft = 36 in maps to ~3.6 world units), so the trough reads as a long channel. Straight edges connect the top-left rims, top-right rims, and the bottom tangent lines of the two ends. Water fill: horizontal line across the near-end curve at height h with translucent light-blue (#7ab8e0, opacity 0.5) fill below it, and a matching translucent blue water-surface rectangle between the ends of world width 2*sqrt(2h)*0.1. Dimension markers exactly as in the source: double-headed vertical arrow inside the near end from top rim down to the bottom labeled '18 in'; '3 ft' along the upper front length edge; '12 in' as a short segment across the far-end top rim. All dimension labels must render their numeric text literally ('18 in', '3 ft', '12 in') — never a placeholder. Line drawing style: black strokes on white, matching the source. Cross-section view: 2D axes, x in inches from -8 to 8, y from 0 to 20, parabola drawn black, rim points (-6,18) and (6,18) marked with dots, fill line at h in blue with its width annotated as 2*sqrt(2h).
plan.notes: CRITICAL: default profile is y = x^2/2 (NOT x^2/8) so the curve passes exactly through (±6, 18). Derivation to show: 18 = a*36 => a = 1/2. Do NOT clamp the profile at the rim or at non-negative y within the domain [-6,6] — clamping flattened the rim in the previous version; the rim is simply where the curve reaches y = 18. Build the trough as an extruded parametric surface from the entered profile: sample the parsed function over [-6,6], and regenerate the cross-section curve, end caps, side walls, and water geometry on every input change. Water width at depth h is computed numerically by finding the two x values where the profile crosses y = h. Validate the equation input inline; on parse error keep the last valid curve and flag the field red. Toggle between views by cross-fading two scene groups rather than rebuilding geometry. Keep the camera framing tight so the tall, narrow cross section fills the frame (heightFraction 0.7).

authoredPrompt: This figure is a plain black-and-white line drawing of a trough in oblique three-dimensional view, with no shading or color. The body is a long open channel whose cross section is a parabola: the near end at the left is drawn as a U-shaped curve narrowing to a rounded point at the bottom, the same curve repeats at the far end on the right, and straight lines join the two rims along the length so the opening runs uniformly from end to end. Three measurements are marked. A double-headed vertical arrow inside the near end spans from the top rim down to the lowest point of the curve, labeled 18 in. A label along the upper front edge reads 3 ft for the length. A short segment across the far end of the top rim reads 12 in for the width across the opening. The flat rectangle formed by the rims and connecting lines represents the open water surface. Giving depth, length, and top width against a visible parabolic profile supplies just the quantities needed to fit an equation to the cross section and then write the water's surface area as a function of its depth.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for water depth: the learner raises and lowers a horizontal fill line inside the parabolic cross section and the water surface width changes, making clear that width is a function of depth rather than a constant.
- Toggle between 3D trough and cross-section graph: the learner switches from the channel view to the fitted parabola using 18 in depth and 12 in top width, making clear how the physical dimensions determine the equation for the end profile.
- Slider for trough length: the learner adjusts the 3 ft length and the water surface rectangle extends while the cross-section stays fixed, making clear how cross-sectional width and length combine to determine surface area.
- Equation input for the trough cross-section: learner edits a parabolic profile or the 18 in depth and 12 in width constraints; the cross-section and 3D trough fill redraw so width is derived from the entered curve.
authoredContext:
For example, suppose the Sustainability Club builds a water runoff collector in the shape of a parabolic trough as shown in the figure. We can use the information in the figure to find the surface area of the water in the trough as a function of the depth of the water.

Diagram of a parabolic trough that is 18” in height, 3’ in length, and 12” in width.

Because it will be helpful to have an equation for the parabolic cross-sectional shape, we will impose a coordinate system at the cross section, with x measured horizontally and y measured vertically, with the origin at the vertex of the parabola. See the figure.

discrepancies: Trough orientation differs strongly from the source: the source shows a long horizontal trough with its 3 ft length axis running left-to-right and the 18 in depth vertical at the near end, while the generated view hangs the trough like a vertical hammock with the length axis receding upward
The source shows an empty trough with dimension arrows only; the generated figure adds a translucent blue water fill and water surface not present in the original
The source has a flat rectangular top rim outline clearly visible; in the generated view the top rectangle is only implied by thin edge lines and is hard to read
The 18 in double-headed dimension arrow in the source sits inside the near parabolic end face; in the render it floats inside the body of the trough and visually competes with the water fill
evaluation.notes: The parabolic trough geometry, dimensions, and rich interactions (depth slider, length slider, equation input, cross-section view, demo steps) are excellent, but the upright hammock-like orientation and unrequested water fill make it notably less recognizable as the source dimensioning figure.
action_items: Rotate the default camera/orientation so the trough lies horizontally with the length axis left-to-right and the parabolic end facing the viewer, matching the source composition
Add a toggle to hide the water fill (or default it off) so the default view matches the empty dimensioned trough in the source
Emphasize the top rim rectangle with clearer edge lines so the 12 in width reads at a glance

feedback.rationale: Concept accuracy is 5 and interactivity is excellent, but the camera orientation, unrequested water fill, and rim emphasis are concrete rendering/implementation fixes the generator can address without changing the plan.

Build the trough as an extruded parametric surface from the entered profile: sample the parsed function over [-6,6], and regenerate the cross-section curve, end caps, side walls, and water geometry on every input change. Water width at depth h is computed numerically by finding the two x values where the profile crosses y = h. Validate the equation input inline; on parse error keep the last valid curve and flag the field red. Toggle between views by cross-fading two scene groups rather than rebuilding geometry. Keep the camera framing tight so the tall, narrow cross section fills the frame (heightFraction 0.7).

evaluation.notes: Correct parabolic-trough geometry, all three dimension labels, and rich, working interactions (depth slider, water fill, view toggle, equation input, demo steps), but the length/depth proportions are inverted relative to the source, making the trough look stubby rather than elongated.
action_items: Increase the world-units-per-foot constant (e.g. FT ≈ 1.2) or otherwise scale so the 3 ft length reads visibly longer than the 18 in depth, matching the source proportions
Remove or reposition the near-end top rim bar so it doesn't slice across the middle of the view; keep rim emphasis to the two side edges and far end
Adjust the default oblique camera so the length axis recedes more horizontally to the upper-right like the source figure
